question: Wolves can be hunted for population management purposes in Sweden and Estonia, but not in Finland. Hunting for population management purposes would also give wolves a fear of humans and help keep wolves away from human settlements. At present, the process for obtaining individual hunting permits is regarded as slow and cumbersome.

The situation of the wolf population also varies around the country and regulation based on a nationwide assessment may have been perceived as unfair locally. For example, according to a report by the Finnish Hunters’ Association, wolf sightings in rural areas of Finland have increased. This has an impact not only on how safe people feel and the keeping of animals outdoors, but also on hunting as a pursuit.

The risk of hunting dogs being killed by wolves is making people less keen to go hunting as a hobby, meaning it is more difficult to manage the elk population. According to the case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, it is possible under the Habitats Directive to hunt wolves for population management purposes, subject to certain conditions.

Regulation concerning wolves should be brought more into line with the current population numbers. In a parliamentary communication (EK 41/2022), the Finnish Parliament has also taken the position that, for the whole of Finland, the wolf should be moved from Annex IV (strictly protected species) of the Habitats Directive to Annex V (protected species). In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider the differences among the Nordic and Baltic countries when it comes to the hunting of wolves for population management to be problematic, and is it possible to enhance the rules to make it easier to start hunting wolves for population management purposes in the Member States?

Is it possible that, also for Finland in general, the wolf could be moved from Annex IV of the Habitats Directive to Annex V, which already covers wolves in the reindeer‑herding area of Northern Finland, and, for example, in Estonia?
answer: 1. Sweden, Finland and Estonia have different levels of legal protection (1) for their wolf populations under the Habitats Directive (2). Consequently, the constraints and the possibilities for wolf culling in the mentioned Member States are not the same. As regards Sweden, an infringement procedure has been opened in 2010 (3) in relation to their wolf management practices.

In Finland, the derogations granted by national authorities under Article 16(1) of the directive to allow killing of wolves have been the subject of a preliminary ruling of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), in Case C674/17 (4), in which all the conditions for such practices have been clearly defined.

On 12 October 2021, the Commission adopted a guidance document (5) providing clarifications of the legal provisions under Articles 12 and 16 of the Habitats Directive and reflecting the latest legal interpretations of the CJEU, including the above-mentioned ruling concerning wolf derogations in Finland. 2.

Following the adoption of the EU proposal (6) to reduce the protection status of the wolf under the Bern Convention (7), after its entry into force, the Commission will present a targeted legislative proposal to implement this change in EU law and to modify accordingly the regime of the wolf under the Habitats Directive, moving the wolf from Annex IV (strict protection) to Annex V (protection).

Protected (Annex V) in Estonia and in the Finnish reindeer management area. Strictly protected (Annex IV) in the rest of Finland and in Sweden.
